$comment: Salary detection, lifted verbatim from apps/ai-service/app/profiling/signals.py.
WHY THIS FILE IS THE RISKIEST ONE IN THE PACKAGE: the period decides a factor of TWELVE.
'2.5 lakh saal ka' is 20,833/month; read as monthly it becomes 250,000 and lands in
salary_expectation.amount_min, on the resume, and in the deterministic ranking factor
reach.mappers.ts reads. Every window width and cue list below was tuned against a real
regression, so treat each number as measured, not as a preference.
THE RULE THE WHOLE FILE OBEYS: prefer NO number over a WRONG number. Ambiguous period,
implausible magnitude, a bare calendar year, a credential id -> record nothing. An
unrecorded salary is re-askable next turn; a fabricated one ships.
$comment_matcher: THE UNIT MUST END ON A WORD BOUNDARY. Without {WE} the bare 'k' alternative matched the
FIRST LETTER of the next Hindi word, so 'NSQF level 4 kiya hai' read the 'k' of 'kiya' as
thousands and recorded a 4,000 salary. Every '<digit> kaam/karta/kiya' phrase did the same.
Identical trap for the bare 'l' in front of any l-word.
DIGITS ARE ENUMERATED as [0-9०-९] rather than \d. This is NOT cosmetic: Python's \d is
Unicode-aware and already matched Devanagari, and float() parses them, so '२५०००' records
25000 on the shipped code today. Writing [0-9] would have silently dropped that; writing
\d would break JavaScript, whose \d is ASCII-only. The enumeration is the only form that
preserves the shipped behaviour in both engines. It does narrow Python for scripts this
corpus does not contain (Bengali, Tamil digits) — narrowing toward agreement is the safe
direction, and the differential over 500 probes shows no change.
The unit alternation is thousandUnits ++ lakhUnits IN THAT ORDER. A test asserts it, so
the lists below and this pattern cannot drift apart.
$comment_thousandUnits: 'hazaar' BEFORE 'hazar', and the order is the whole fix (R12 1.1, measured 2026-08-28).
The list held only 'hazar', so '22 hazaar' — the ordinary spelling — recorded NOTHING. The
mechanism is the {WE} word-end guard doing its job: 'hazar' matches the first five
characters, {WE} sees the second 'a' and refuses, the optional unit group settles for empty,
and minDigitsWithoutUnit then drops the bare two-digit number. A worker's whole salary
answer disappears and nothing logs a reason.
Alternation is first-match-wins, so a longer spelling must precede the prefix it contains.
Backtracking would in fact recover here — the engine retries the remaining alternatives
after {WE} fails — but relying on that is relying on an optimisation detail across two
regex engines. Longest-first is the rule; keep it.
STILL UNCOVERED and deliberately not added, because 1.1 ruled one spelling: 'hajar' (j for
z) and 'hazzar'. test_salary_attribution.py carries them as pinned gaps with their measured
behaviour, so adding either is a one-line change that a red test then confirms.
$comment_minDigitsWithoutUnit: A bare 1-2 digit number with no unit is almost always years, not rupees ('5 saal'), so it
is skipped before any other test runs. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, pinned by a test: '5 lpa' and
'5 LPA chahiye' therefore record NOTHING, even though 'lpa' is an annual cue — the number
is dropped before the period is ever consulted. Widening this is a product decision with a
fabrication risk on the other side of it, not a bug fix.
$comment_maxPlausibleInr: The ceiling is SHARED with the pseudonymizer's D-1 money carve-out. pseudonymize.py holds
MAX_PLAUSIBLE_SALARY_INR and remains the single source of truth; signals.py raises at
import if this value disagrees with it, so the copy the TypeScript side needs can never
drift into a masking decision the gateway did not make.
$comment_periodWindow: Read in a TIGHT window around the amount — wide enough for '1.5 lakh saal ka', narrow
enough that the '5 saal' of an experience clause elsewhere in the same sentence cannot
mark an unrelated amount as annual.
$comment_expectedCues: R15 3.1 - THESE ARE MATCHED AT A WORD START, NOT AS BARE SUBSTRINGS.
`chah` used to be written ` chah`, with a LEADING SPACE, so the stem could not fire inside a
longer word. A space is a proxy for `word start` and it is wrong at both ends of the string:
an utterance that OPENS with the ask has no character before the cue at all, so `chah raha hu
30000 mahina` carried NO expectation cue and the asking price was filed as the current pay.
Measured on a 2,200-row sweep whose every row opens with the cue: 440 of them wrong, and the
gap is older than every guard in this file.
The boundary is a LETTER test rather than an alphanumeric one, deliberately. `(a')` clamps the
backward window to the end of the previous NUMBER, so the character before a cue is a digit
whenever that clamp fires; treating a digit as a word character would have made the new rule
silently undo the guard R14 added one packet ago.
The rule applies to EVERY cue, which also stops `expect` matching inside `unexpected` - a
second-order fix nobody had asked for, and the reason the sweeps below are reported in both
directions rather than only where the change was aimed.
SUBSTRINGS, not patterns — matched with a plain containment test against the lowercased
window, exactly as signals.py does. ' chah' carries a LEADING SPACE on purpose: it is a
stem catching 'chah raha hu' / 'chahta hu' without firing inside an unrelated word.
$comment_expectedAnchor: THE PERIOD-ANCHORED EXTENSION, AND THE THREE GUARDS THAT MAKE IT SAFE (R13 1.1).
THE DEFECT. expectedWindowAfter is 10 characters measured from the END of the number, so
any period word sitting between the amount and its cue eats the window: '35000 mahina
chahiye' has 8 characters of ' mahina' before ' chahiye' even begins. The cue is never
seen, the amount falls through to the CURRENT slot, and a worker's ASKING PRICE is printed
on his resume as what he already earns — his negotiating floor, advertised. Measured on
five natural phrasings: mahina, per month, mahine ki, saal ka, per annum.
THE FIX. When the base window finds no cue, re-anchor the window's END after the period
phrase and look again. The width does not change; only where it starts from.
WHY THAT ALONE IS NOT SHIPPABLE, MEASURED. 'abhi 25000 mahina, 30k chahiye' is one worker
answering both salary questions in a breath. Re-anchored, 25000's window now reaches
' chah' — so the CURRENT pay is recorded as EXPECTED and the real asking price is dropped
as a duplicate by first-writer-wins. That is the exact regression this file's line clamp
was added to prevent, re-created at a different range. A 7,150-utterance combinatorial
sweep (13 period words x 11 separators x 5 second amounts x 5 cues x 2 cue positions)
measured it at 1,776 utterances where the naked anchor moves a today-correct reading to a
wrong one.
THE THREE GUARDS. Regressions over the same sweep, each guard measured ALONE and then in
combination — because 'this one is the important one' is exactly the kind of claim that
survives a 43-row probe list and dies on 7,150:
naked anchor, no guards ................ 1776
(a) never extend across the next NUMBER  1520
(b) never extend across a clause end .... 907
(c) a number AFTER the cue owns the cue .. 256
NO SINGLE GUARD IS SUFFICIENT and none is redundant. (c) is the strongest alone and still
leaves 256: in 'abhi 25000 mahina, chahiye 30k' the cue is FRONTED — Hindi routinely puts
it before its number — so only 'somebody else's number is standing behind this cue' tells
the two apart, and where the second number is missing entirely only the clamps do.
The extension is never SHORTER than today's window (`max(base_end, limit)`), so no
phrasing that works today can stop working through this path.
WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX, and this is measured too: '30000-35000 mahina chahiye' becomes
(30000 current, 35000 expected) — a stated BAND read as two independent figures. Guard (a)
is what stops the band's lower end reaching the cue. A clause-clamp-only variant happens
to get that one right and regresses four other probes, so it is the wrong trade. The band
shape is pinned as its own class in test_salary_attribution.py; it needs a range rule, not
a wider window.
── R14 2.2 — THE SAME DEFECT, POINTING BACKWARDS ─────────────────────────────────────
Everything above guards the window's END. Nothing guarded its START, and the window before
an amount is 25 characters — two and a half times the forward one. So when a worker states
the ASK FIRST, '35000 chahiye, abhi 25000 milta hai', the current pay's backward window
still reaches the ask's cue, the current pay is marked EXPECTED, and first-writer-wins then
discards it. His actual wage vanishes from the profile entirely.
THE SWEEP COULD NOT SEE IT, AND THAT IS THE POINT. R13's grid is
`abhi 25000 <period><sep> <tail>` — every one of its 7,150 rows states the current pay
first. A generated corpus tests the generator's assumptions. A SECOND sweep of the same
size with the ask stated first is what produced the numbers below.
TWO GUARDS, MIRRORING (a) AND (b). Measured on the reversed sweep, monthly-period rows
only (4,400 — an annual '25000 saal ka' normalises to ₹2,083 and is a different question):
shipped, no start guard ...... 872 of 4400 record the current pay correctly
(a') clamp at the PREVIOUS number ....... +1248 recovered on the full 7,150
(b') clamp at the last clause end ....... +1360
(a') + (b')  <- shipped ....... 2968 of 4400 correct, +2096 recovered, 0 regressions
Zero regressions on BOTH sweeps, and the expected-salary slot is byte-identical across all
14,300 rows — this can only ever move a number out of the wrong slot, never out of a right
one. There is no (c') because (a') subsumes it: clamping at the previous number's end
leaves no number inside the backward window for a cue to belong to.
THE RESIDUAL, PINNED NOT FIXED: 992 of 4,400 still lose the current pay, and every one is
the same shape — NO separator at all between the two clauses, '30k chahiye abhi 25000
mahina milta hai'. Neither clamp fires: the cue trails the ask directly and there is no
punctuation. Closing it needs an ADJACENCY rule (a cue belongs to the number it touches),
which is a different mechanism from a clamp and is pinned as its own row.
$comment_annualCues: ASYMMETRIC ON PURPOSE. AFTER the amount a bare 'saal' is the annual marker ('1.5 lakh saal
ka'). BEFORE it, a bare 'saal' is far more likely to be the EXPERIENCE clause ('5 saal se
25000 milta hai') — reading that as annual would divide a correct monthly wage by twelve,
trading one wrong number for another. So the before-set carries only unambiguously annual
words. Deleting a cue from the after-set or adding 'saal' to the before-set are both 12x
errors; the corpus pins each direction.
$comment_subMonthlyCues: A DAILY OR WEEKLY WAGE IS RECORDED AS NOTHING, NEVER AS A MONTHLY ONE (R14 2.1).
THE DEFECT THIS CLOSES, measured R13 1.3 and pinned as `daily_wage`. The period DEFAULTED
instead of being consulted: `_period_months` returns 1 when it finds no cue, so
'1200 daily milta hai' recorded ₹1,200 A MONTH for a man earning roughly ₹31,000 — a
twenty-sixth of his wage, printed on his résumé under a label an employer reads as his
current pay. This file's premise is 'prefer NO number over a WRONG number' and on this one
shape it did the opposite, by a factor of twenty-six, in the direction that costs the worker.
SUPPRESSION, NOT CONVERSION, AND THAT NEEDS NO PRODUCT RULING. Multiplying by a days-per-month
figure would put a number on the sheet that nobody stated — 26 days, 30 days and 24 days are
all defensible and they differ by 25%. Returning None is the SAME degrade the annual/monthly
CONFLICT already takes, and it is what the pinned row's `want` has said since it was written.
WHY THE R-2 UNDER-REPRESENTATION GATE COULD NOT SEE IT. That gate compares a STATED scalar
against a DERIVED one and forbids the derived one being lower. Here both are 1200: the sheet
prints the stated number unchanged. The error is in the UNIT, and the unit never crosses the
contract — no writer anywhere produces the ₹31,000 the gate would need to compare against.
It is a detector-layer defect and this is the only layer that can see it.
`day` AND `din` ARE DELIBERATELY BROAD. Either can appear near an amount without meaning a
daily wage, and the cost of a false positive here is that a number is not recorded — the
failure direction this file already chooses everywhere else. The cost of a false NEGATIVE is
a 26x under-statement on a worker's résumé. Measured before shipping: zero change across the
531-row shared corpus and the 7,150-utterance sweep.
`ro[zj](?:ana|aana)?{WE}` — the trailing boundary is what keeps 'rozgar' (employment, a word
that genuinely appears in these transcripts) out of the daily set.
$comment_moneyCues: What makes a bare 4-digit number MONEY rather than a calendar year. ANCHORED patterns, not
substrings: a loose 'rs' would fire on the 'rs' inside 'years' and turn every '2012 years'
KNOWN AND DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED: 'ctc' is a money cue but NOT an annual cue, so 'ctc 4
lakh' records ₹4,00,000 per MONTH. CTC is annual in ordinary Indian usage, which makes
this the 12x error this file exists to prevent, pointing the other way. It is shipped
behaviour and is pinned by a corpus case; changing it is a product call, not a port.
$comment_credentialBefore: A number sitting immediately after a CREDENTIAL cue is not money. Measured 2026-07-22:
'NCVT hai, roll number R/2019/123456' recorded a 123,456 salary and 'certificate number
4471 hai' recorded 4,471 — both flowed to salary_expectation.amount_min and onto the
resume. The detector is topic-blind and only rejects amounts under 1,000, so a roll number
is indistinguishable from a wage to it.
PROXIMITY, not a line scan and not a fixed character window — both looser rules shipped
false suppressions. Scanning the LINE dropped both salaries from 'abhi 25000 milta hai,
35000 chahiye, NCVT certificate hai' (one worker answering several questions in one
message, and a chat message is a single line), and a 30-character window still dropped the
salary from 'NCVT certificate hai, abhi 25000 milta hai'.
The gap between cue and digits may be the REST OF THE IDENTIFIER — 'roll number
R/2019/123456' reaches its last digit run through 'R/2019/'. Identifier characters only,
so a space or comma ends the run and an unrelated later number is not suppressed.
'$' IS SAFE IN BOTH ENGINES HERE. Python's '$' also matches before a trailing newline
while JavaScript's does not, but this pattern is only ever applied to the slice between
the start of the number's own line and the number, which by construction contains no
newline. The '-' sits last inside each character class so neither engine reads a range,
and so no '\-' escape is needed (it is a SyntaxError in a JavaScript u-mode pattern).
